# Types of brackets

BPL has three kinds of bracket: brackets `[ ]`, parentheses `( )` and braces `{ }`. Each gives its own meaning to the separators inside it: a space, `;`, `⋄` and a line break. This page covers those meanings. [Arrays](arrays.qmd) covers the vectors and arrays that brackets write, and [Dfns](dfns.qmd) covers the functions that braces define.

| Inside | Space | `;` | `⋄` | Line break |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `[ ]` | Separates items | Separates items that contain spaces | Separates rows of an array | Counts as a space |
| `( )` | Separates runs | Not allowed | Separates rows of a vector | Counts as a space |
| `{ }` | Separates runs | Separates bodies | Separates statements | Separates statements |
| Top level | Separates runs | Not allowed | Separates statements | Separates statements |

A [run](rules.qmd#term-run) is a sequence of tokens with no spaces between them. [Reading expressions](rules.qmd#reading-expressions) gives the rules for runs.

## Brackets

Brackets are used to write vectors. Inside brackets, spaces separate items, so each run is one item. Items are evaluated left to right.

```bpl
a←1 ⋄ b←2
[a b]              ⍝ 1 2
[a+b a×b]          ⍝ 3 2
[c←1 c+1]          ⍝ 1 2
```

An item that needs spaces goes in parentheses. When several items need spaces, separate the items with `;` instead. Then only `;` separates items, and inside each item spaces separate runs, as they do outside brackets.

```bpl
x←2 4 9
[(+/x) ≢x]         ⍝ 15 3ₓ
[+/x ; +/x ÷ ≢x]   ⍝ 15 5
```

With `⋄`, brackets write an array whose major cells are the rows. Rows of different lengths are padded with fill. A line break inside brackets counts as a space, so a matrix written over several lines needs `⋄` at the end of each row. One pair of brackets can't use both `;` and `⋄`.

```bpl
[1 2 ⋄ 3 4 5]      ⍝ [1 2 0 ⋄ 3 4 5]
m←[1 2 3 ⋄
   4 5 6]
⍴m                 ⍝ [2 3]ₓ
```

Brackets don't index. [Index](glyphs/squad.qmd) `⌷` selects, and a [subscript](scripts.qmd#subscripts) selects one position.

## Parentheses

Parentheses group one expression. Inside them, spaces separate runs, as at the top level. A line break counts as a space, so one expression can continue over several lines.

```bpl
(2×3)+4            ⍝ 10
total←(1+2
       × 3+4)
total              ⍝ 21
```

With `⋄`, parentheses write a vector of rows. Each row is a vector, even a row with one item, and rows can differ in length. In brackets, the same rows would form one array.

```bpl
(4 ⋄ 4 5)          ⍝ [[4] [4 5]]
[4 ⋄ 4 5]          ⍝ [4 0 ⋄ 4 5]
```

## Braces

Braces define a function. Inside braces, `⋄` and line breaks separate statements, and spaces separate runs. `;` separates bodies. When a body's predicate `C?` is false, evaluation moves on to the next body.

```bpl
{x←⍵ ⋄ x+1}2       ⍝ 3
{⍵<0?-⍵;⍵}¯3       ⍝ 3
```

## The top level

Outside any bracket, `⋄` and line breaks separate statements, and spaces separate runs. A `;` outside brackets and braces is a `SYNTAX` error.
